sealed_thresholds.note: registered BEFORE measurement; never tuned to results (Art. XXVII)
sealed_thresholds.ensemble: NONE (single-attacker calibration only; majority-vote ensembles are deferred by the R412 directive)

escalation.reason: measured FPR 1.0 > sealed bar 0.3 (Art. L: the attacker is measured non-selective; its KILL is inadmissible as a terminal verdict and is escalated with the objection preserved)
escalation.rule: the instrument's KILL is measured non-selective (FPR above the sealed bar); the objection is preserved verbatim and ESCALATED for adjudication — the candidate is NOT killed by this attack alone (Art. L); the deterministic gates are unchanged

preserved_objections.basis: The adaptive request migration mechanism fails to address the fundamental bit-flip vulnerability of shared KV-cache blocks as documented in evidence [doi:10.5220/0015138800004103], which shows that migration introduces data corruption risks that would worsen the very problem it aims to solve

The mechanism violates the boundary condition of "diverse resource conditions" by assuming predictable migration capacity, contradicting evidence [doi:10.70675/036b4171z0acfz4a50z9d51z481b92e5f4da] which demonstrates fundamental limits of shared-cache networks under unpredictable conditions

The candidate's prediction of reduced live-token evictions directly contradicts evidence [doi:10.1109/icassp55912.2026.11461518] which shows that MIDAS, a similar cross-GPU KV cache framework, actually increases eviction rates during burst conditions due to migration overhead

The mechanism cannot outperform the baseline during traffic peaks because the claimed 30% reduction in live-token evictions fails to account for the migration overhead that evidence [doi:10.14711/thesis-hdl152583] shows increases latency by 40-60% during high-frequency migrations

The scheduling algorithm cannot be implemented as claimed because evidence [doi:10.5463/thesis.308] demonstrates that latency-critical inference serving requires deterministic scheduling, which is incompatible with the proposed variable migration count that introduces scheduling unpredictability

The testable prediction fails to pin down the critical measurement of migration frequency versus eviction reduction, making it impossible to validate whether the 30% improvement is net-positive after accounting for the migration cost that evidence shows scales non-linearly with request diversity
